nameStory: Purple Heart gets its name from the stunning deep purple color that dominates nearly every part of the plant - stems, leaves, and even the undersides of foliage all show rich violet hues. The heart-shaped leaves and the plant's tendency to 'bleed' purple sap when cut add to this colorful common name. It's also called Purple Queen, reflecting its regal appearance in gardens and containers.
description: Purple Heart is a trailing perennial plant with striking deep purple foliage that's become a popular ornamental in New England gardens and containers. This low-growing plant spreads along the ground with succulent-like stems that can reach 1-2 feet long, creating a colorful carpet effect. Originally from Mexico's Gulf Coast, it's grown here as an annual or houseplant since it can't survive New England winters outdoors. The entire plant has an almost magical purple glow that makes it instantly recognizable.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval, pointed leaves are deep purple on top with even more intense purple undersides. The leaves feel slightly thick and fleshy, like a succulent, and are arranged alternately along the stem.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in a trailing, spreading manner with stems that bend and cascade. The plant forms dense mats as it spreads, with stems that root where they touch soil.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small three-petaled pink or purple flowers appear at stem tips, each about half an inch across. The delicate flowers have a simple, triangular appearance typical of spiderworts.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Purple stems are smooth and somewhat succulent-feeling, with visible joints or nodes where leaves attach. When broken, stems release a clear to slightly purple sap.

habitat: In New England, Purple Heart is found exclusively in cultivated settings - garden beds, containers, hanging baskets, and as indoor houseplants. You might spot it in summer flower displays, municipal plantings, or cascading from window boxes in urban and suburban areas. Since it's not cold-hardy here, any outdoor populations are temporary seasonal plantings that won't survive winter.

seasonality.spring: Appears in garden centers and outdoor plantings after last frost, showing vibrant purple foliage. New growth is especially intense in color.
seasonality.summer: At its peak beauty with full purple foliage and occasional small pink flowers. This is when it's most commonly seen in New England landscapes and containers.
seasonality.fall: Outdoor plants begin declining with first frost, though container plants may be brought indoors. Foliage may become even more intensely purple in cool weather.
seasonality.winter: Only survives indoors as a houseplant in New England. Indoor plants may become leggy and lose some purple intensity in lower light conditions.

funFact: Purple Heart is actually a natural air purifier that scientists have discovered can remove harmful chemicals like formaldehyde and benzene from indoor air, making this beautiful plant a functional addition to your home as well as decorative!
confusionNotes: The deep purple foliage makes Purple Heart quite distinctive, but it might be confused with other purple-leaved ornamentals like purple-leafed sweet potato vine. Purple Heart's succulent-like stems and the spiderwort family's characteristic three-petaled flowers help distinguish it - remember 'three petals for the purple heart.'
contextualKnowledge: Though called Purple Heart, this plant is completely unrelated to the Purple Heart flower (Soldanella) or military decoration. It's worth noting that this Mexican native has only been widely available in New England gardens since the late 20th century, so older field guides may not include it.
compareHints: Unlike its native New England spiderwort cousins like Virginia spiderwort, Purple Heart has distinctly purple foliage year-round rather than green leaves. Virginia spiderwort is also much more upright and hardy, while Purple Heart trails and spreads. The other common houseplant relative, inchplant, has striped silver and green leaves instead of solid purple, helping distinguish between these popular indoor spiderworts.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Virginia spiderwort is the most common spiderwort in New England and has the classic blue-purple flowers and smooth leaves.
Ohio spiderwort differs from Virginia spiderwort mainly in its hairless sepals and slightly more robust growth habit.

Compared to Virginia spiderwort (the most common spiderwort in New England), longbract spiderwort has much longer bracts extending well beyond the flower clusters, while Ohio spiderwort has hairless leaves (longbract's are slightly hairy).
Unlike our native Virginia spiderwort with its grass-like leaves and blue flowers, inchplant has broad, striped leaves and rarely flowers indoors.
